Modules: CommonJS vs. ES Modules

Two ways Node files share code with each other, and which one this project uses.

A Laravel app never really asks "how does this file get code from that file?" — Composer's autoloader and PHP's use statements handle it invisibly. Node makes the choice explicit, and there are actually two competing module systems:

  • CommonJS — Node's original system: require('./thing') to import, module.exports = ... to export. You'll see this in a lot of older Node tutorials and StackOverflow answers.
  • ES Modules (ESM) — the module syntax that's part of the JavaScript language itself (the same import/export you may have seen used with a bundler like Webpack for frontend code): import thing from './thing.js' and export default ... / export const ....
// CommonJS (not used in this project)
const express = require('express');
module.exports = someFunction;

// ES Modules (what this project uses)
import express from 'express';
export default someFunction;

package.json's "type": "module" field (Figure 1.1, previous slide) is what tells Node to treat every .js file in this project as an ES Module rather than CommonJS — without it, Node assumes CommonJS by default. This project intentionally uses ES Modules throughout, since it's the modern, language-standard syntax and the same one used on the frontend.

One ESM rule that trips people up coming from other languages: relative imports must include the file extension. Figure 1.2 shows this in the file you'll meet properly next lesson-topic — note './routes/index.js', not './routes/index'.

// Figure 1.2: relative imports include the .js extension (src/app.js, excerpt)
import express from 'express';
import routes from './routes/index.js';
import notFound from './middleware/notFound.js';
import errorHandler from './middleware/errorHandler.js';

Note express itself is imported with no relative path and no extension — that's how you import a package installed into node_modules/, versus your own files which are always a relative path (./ or ../) starting from the current file.
